newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa's foreign borrowing - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa's foreign borrowing - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

With the release of the October Exchequer Account statement in the Government Gazette it has become possible to piece together the saga of the German public loans, which demonstrates the absurdity of a country with a chronically depreciating currency borrowing abroad.

The exercise had not been straightforward because of some faulty accounting by the Department of State Expenditure in 1991 when the 1991-1996 loan was reflected in the Exchequer returns as having been received in two parts in October and December of that year. This has been a source of confusion.
It has now become clear that the 400 million Deutschmark loan was raised in October but part, more than half, was invested abroad in preparation for the redemption of the 1983-1991 loan in December.

The full value of the loan in October should have been reflected in the October statement. Furthermore the apparent loan receipts shown for December included the capital profits from a further depreciated rand since the October valuation date.

Well, the story begins with the venture into the German market for the first time in 1983. An eight year market loan of DM200 million was raised in December of that year with a coupon of 8.5 percent. At the exchange rate of 44 rand cents to the mark, the loan was valued at 88.3 million rand.
In his budget speech the following March the Minister of Finance, Owen Horwood, stated:

"If further proof of the country's high credit rating were needed, it was provided by the loans we have successfully raised in recent months in four major and prestigious foreign markets...the first three of these loans were in the form of public bond issues; that is they were raised in the full glare of international publicity.

"To avoid any semblance of over-borrowing, the amounts per loan have been kept to modest proportions, but they have served to maintain South Africa's presence in the capital markets of the world and to prove our creditworthiness where it matters."
One cannot resist the funny part where he went on to say:

"Our credit rating abroad has been enhanced in recent years not only by our conservative approach to monetary and fiscal management but also by the positive reaction to the new constitutional dispensation and the visionary peace initiatives of the hon the Prime Minister."

Unfortunately the rand had already begun to slide very badly and the costliness in rand terms of foreign borrowing should have been more than apparent to the Ministry of Finance. And yet they went ahead and borrowed a further DM200 million in December 1984, but at an improved coupon rate of 7.75 percent.

Although the Minister still prattled on about the country's good overseas credit rating in the 1985 budget speech, this further borrowing may have been raised to bolster the foreign exchange reserves which were being severely tested because of the depressed gold price. The rand had depreciated against the dollar by 54 percent between September 1983 and January 1985, after which there was a temporary strengthening until the sky fell in later that year.

By the time the 1983-91 Deutschmark loan was redeemed in December 1991 the exchange rate had weakened against the mark from 44 rand cents to 177 cents, that is exactly four times. The rand redemption value was 353 million rand, as opposed to the original book value of 88 million rand.
Of course the annual interest payments of DM17 million had become incrasingly more costly in rands each year.

If the full costs of the 1983-91 loan were to take both interest and forex capital cost into account the total in rands amounted to 440 million rand, which represents an average annual service cost of 62.3 percent. The worst imputed service cost taking interest and progressive capital costs into account happened in 1985 when the rate was 95 percent.

The loan of the following year, the 1984-92, fared much better at an average service cost of 34.5 percent by the time of redemption. The original 148.8 million rand raised against the DM200 million in December 1984 had to be redeemed at a rand cost of 381 million rand in December 1992.

Of course, by the time of redemption of the first Deutschmark loan South Africa was on the treadmill of foreign borrowing. Foreign exchange reserves were low at the end of the first year of economic recovery and the only option was to borrow in order to redeem. The 1991-1996 Deutschmark loan was upped to DM400 million for market conditions were favourably disposed to South Africa and it was the right amount to meet the 1983-1991 loan and the 1984-1992 loan coming up the following year.

This 1991-96 loan was valued at 682.5 million rand and has just been redeemed this last October at 1,196 million rand, at a forex capital loss of 513.6 million rand. But this time the average service cost over five years had been much more respectable at 29.7 percent, despite the dramatic slide of the rand this year. The imputed service cost this past year works out at 42.4 percent.

The 1991-96 loan has been replaced by the latest Deutschmark borrowing, the 1996-2000 four year loan. Originally intended to be DM400 million it was raised to 500 million because of favourable market conditions -- a fulsome coupon rate of seven percent and no currency risk to the German public.

Actually because of a small market premium DM508 million has been raised and the rand valuation that appears in the October Exchequer return is 1,491 million rand. The difference between this capital revenue and the redemption cost of the loan replaced, amounting to some 295 million rand, will have been used to pay the last instalment of interest amounting to 125 million rand with the rest going into foreign reserves -- for the time being because there is the ECU loan of 800 million rand, book value, to be redeemed in February next year.

Thus with an initial modest nibble in the German bond market amounting to 88 million rand South Africa has ended, at this stage, with a liability of nearly 1.5 billion rand. There is no evidence of South Africa having gained anything from this excursion. The loans have never been used to procure anything. They have simply gone into foreign exchange reserves but effectively to be drained to meet interest costs. And yet there are still people who experience a frisson of foreign borrowing.
It is comforting to know that we as a third world country give succour to the developed countries of the world.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
